title: FLea: Addressing Data Scarcity and Label Skew in Federated Learning via Privacy-preserving Feature Augmentation

problem.claim: Federated learning must handle scarce and label-skewed data distributed across devices, which can cause local overfitting and model drift that hinder global-model performance.

gap.claim: Existing federated-learning methods do not adequately address the combined challenges of local data scarcity and label skew across devices.

contributions.claim: FLea uses a global feature buffer containing activation-target pairs shared by multiple clients to support local training and mitigate drift caused by missing classes.
FLea augments local training data through mix-ups between local and global activations to enlarge training samples and reduce local overfitting risk.
FLea obfuscates intermediate activations to reduce their correlation with source data and enhance the privacy of shared features.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report experiments across a wide range of data modalities and simulated levels of local data scarcity and label skew.
The authors report that FLea outperforms state-of-the-art federated-learning counterparts in 13 of 18 settings, with improvements above 5% in those settings.
The authors report concurrent mitigation of privacy vulnerabilities associated with shared features.

narrative_sequence.summary: Federated learning develops models from data distributed across edge devices without transferring local data to a central server.
Scarce and label-skewed device data can produce local overfitting and drift, reducing global-model performance.
FLea introduces a global feature buffer, activation mix-ups, and activation obfuscation to address drift, overfitting, and privacy risks.
The authors evaluate FLea across multiple data modalities and simulated scarcity and label-skew conditions.
The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art counterparts in most tested settings alongside privacy-vulnerability mitigation.

source_observation.claim: A shared global feature buffer and local-global activation mix-ups are used to compensate for missing classes and limited local samples.

interpretation.claim: Sharing privacy-protected intermediate representations may improve local training when client data distributions are sparse or imbalanced.

application.claim: Consider privacy-preserving representation sharing and cross-source augmentation when distributed clients have insufficient or skewed labeled data.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach is effective outside the reported modalities, scarcity levels, or label-skew conditions.

unknowns: Datasets, modalities, baselines, and evaluation metrics are unspecified.
The privacy vulnerabilities assessed and the obfuscation procedure are unspecified.
The experimental conditions and absolute performance values are unspecified.
